claim: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) can be impacted by dietary, environmental, and genetic factors.
source: Inflammatory gut disorders, including inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), can be impacted by dietary, environmental, and genetic factors.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established context for the study.

claim: The incidence of IBD is increasing worldwide.
source: While the incidence of IBD is increasing worldwide, we still lack a complete understanding of the gene-by-environment interactions underlying inflammation and IBD.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations in the introduction section referencing Alatab et al., 2020 and Freeman et al., 2021.

claim: A subset of BXD strains exhibit an IBD-like transcriptome signature on HFD.
source: Here, we profiled the colon transcriptome of 52 BXD mouse strains fed with a chow or high-fat diet (HFD) and identified a subset of BXD strains that exhibit an IBD-like transcriptome signature on HFD, indicating that an interplay of genetics and diet can significantly affect intestinal inflammation.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's transcriptome profiling and enrichment analyses.

claim: IBD-related modules share cis-regulatory elements that are responsive to the STAT2, SMAD3, and REL transcription factors.
source: Using gene co-expression analyses, we identified modules that are enriched for IBD-dysregulated genes and found that these IBD-related modules share cis-regulatory elements that are responsive to the STAT2, SMAD3, and REL transcription factors.
evidence: This finding is based on transcription factor enrichment analysis performed on IBD-related modules.

claim: Muc4 and Epha6 are the top candidates mediating differences in HFD-driven intestinal inflammation.
source: Through a prioritization scheme involving systems genetics in the mouse and integration with external human datasets, we identified Muc4 and Epha6 as the top candidates mediating differences in HFD-driven intestinal inflammation.
evidence: This conclusion is based on ModQTL analysis, literature mining, and GWAS validation in UKBB.

claim: MUC4 and EPHA6 may mediate IBD susceptibility in humans.
source: This work provides insights into the contribution of genetics and diet to IBD risk and identifies two candidate genes, MUC4 and EPHA6, that may mediate IBD susceptibility in humans.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on mouse systems genetics and human GWAS data integration.

claim: A long-term lipid-rich diet is associated with obesity.
source: A long-term lipid-rich diet is associated with multiple metabolic disorders, such as obesity (Hasegawa et al., 2020), cardiovascular disease (Lutsey et al., 2008; Maurya et al., 2023), and systemic low-grade inflammation (Duan et al., 2018; Christ et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Hasegawa et al., 2020.

claim: A long-term lipid-rich diet is associated with cardiovascular disease.
source: A long-term lipid-rich diet is associated with multiple metabolic disorders, such as obesity (Hasegawa et al., 2020), cardiovascular disease (Lutsey et al., 2008; Maurya et al., 2023), and systemic low-grade inflammation (Duan et al., 2018; Christ et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Lutsey et al., 2008 and Maurya et al., 2023.

claim: A long-term lipid-rich diet is associated with systemic low-grade inflammation.
source: A long-term lipid-rich diet is associated with multiple metabolic disorders, such as obesity (Hasegawa et al., 2020), cardiovascular disease (Lutsey et al., 2008; Maurya et al., 2023), and systemic low-grade inflammation (Duan et al., 2018; Christ et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Duan et al., 2018 and Christ et al., 2019.

claim: The gastrointestinal tract is the primary site of adaptation to dietary challenge due to its roles in nutrient absorption, immunity, and metabolism.
source: The gastrointestinal tract is the primary site of adaptation to dietary challenge due to its roles in nutrient absorption, immunity, and metabolism (Enriquez et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Enriquez et al., 2022.

claim: Dietary challenges or other environmental or genetic factors can lead to prolonged inflammation and eventually damage the gastrointestinal tract.
source: Dietary challenges or other environmental or genetic factors can lead to prolonged inflammation and eventually damage the gastrointestinal tract (Huang et al., 2017; Enriquez et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Huang et al., 2017 and Enriquez et al., 2022.

claim: IBD encompasses several chronic inflammatory gut disorders, including ulcerative colitis (UC) and Crohn's disease (CDs).
source: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) encompasses several chronic inflammatory gut disorders, including ulcerative colitis (UC) and Crohn's disease (CDs) (Chang, 2020; Adolph et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a definitional statement supported by citations to Chang, 2020 and Adolph et al., 2022.

claim: Patients with IBD have a higher risk of developing colorectal cancer (CRC).
source: Patients with IBD have a higher risk of developing colorectal cancer (CRC), one of the most lethal cancers (Kim and Chang, 2014; Shah and Itzkowitz, 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Kim and Chang, 2014 and Shah and Itzkowitz, 2022.

claim: The incidence of IBD has increased worldwide during the last decade in part due to increased consumption of lipid-rich diets.
source: The incidence of IBD has increased worldwide (Alatab et al., 2020; Freeman et al., 2021) during the last decade in part due to increased consumption of lipid-rich diets (Maconi et al., 2010; Hou et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Alatab et al., 2020; Freeman et al., 2021; Maconi et al., 2010; and Hou et al., 2011.

claim: High-fat diet (HFD) leads to more inflammation in the dextran sulfate sodium (DSS)-induced UC models compared to normal diet.
source: Furthermore, mouse studies show that high-fat diet (HFD) leads to more inflammation in the dextran sulfate sodium (DSS)-induced UC models compared to normal diet (Zhao et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Zhao et al., 2020.

claim: The response to HFD is variable across individuals.
source: However, the response to HFD is variable across individuals (Zeevi et al., 2015) and the association between the lipid-rich diet and the risk of IBD in clinical studies is inconclusive (Kreuter, 2019), possibly due to genetic factors underlying inter-individual variability in gut inflammation and dysbiosis (Baumgart and Sandborn, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Zeevi et al., 2015.

claim: The association between the lipid-rich diet and the risk of IBD in clinical studies is inconclusive.
source: However, the response to HFD is variable across individuals (Zeevi et al., 2015) and the association between the lipid-rich diet and the risk of IBD in clinical studies is inconclusive (Kreuter, 2019), possibly due to genetic factors underlying inter-individual variability in gut inflammation and dysbiosis (Baumgart and Sandborn, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Kreuter, 2019.

claim: More than 200 risk genes associated with IBD were identified through human genome-wide association studies (GWAS).
source: More than 200 risk genes associated with IBD were identified through human genome-wide association studies (GWAS) (Huang et al., 2017), which have implicated epithelial function, microbe sensing and restriction, and adaptive immune response as drivers (Graham and Xavier, 2020; Kong et al., 2023).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Huang et al., 2017.

claim: IBD GWAS have implicated epithelial function, microbe sensing and restriction, and adaptive immune response as drivers.
source: More than 200 risk genes associated with IBD were identified through human genome-wide association studies (GWAS) (Huang et al., 2017), which have implicated epithelial function, microbe sensing and restriction, and adaptive immune response as drivers (Graham and Xavier, 2020; Kong et al., 2023).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Graham and Xavier, 2020 and Kong et al., 2023.

claim: There is still no effective treatment for IBD.
source: However, there is still no effective treatment for IBD.
evidence: This is a general statement about the current state of IBD treatment.

claim: Anti-tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNF-α) antibodies can temporarily alleviate inflammation in a subset of IBD patients.
source: Current therapies, such as anti-tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNF-α) antibodies (Rutgeerts et al., 2005) and integrin α4β7 antibodies, blocking leukocyte migration (Feagan et al., 2013), can temporarily alleviate inflammation in a subset of patients (Rutgeerts et al., 2005; Feagan et al., 2013) but cause adverse effects (Harbord et al., 2017) and fail to prevent relapses (Doherty et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Rutgeerts et al., 2005 and Feagan et al., 2013.

claim: Integrin α4β7 antibodies, blocking leukocyte migration, can temporarily alleviate inflammation in a subset of IBD patients.
source: Current therapies, such as anti-tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNF-α) antibodies (Rutgeerts et al., 2005) and integrin α4β7 antibodies, blocking leukocyte migration (Feagan et al., 2013), can temporarily alleviate inflammation in a subset of patients (Rutgeerts et al., 2005; Feagan et al., 2013) but cause adverse effects (Harbord et al., 2017) and fail to prevent relapses (Doherty et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Feagan et al., 2013.

claim: Current IBD therapies cause adverse effects.
source: Current therapies, such as anti-tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNF-α) antibodies (Rutgeerts et al., 2005) and integrin α4β7 antibodies, blocking leukocyte migration (Feagan et al., 2013), can temporarily alleviate inflammation in a subset of patients (Rutgeerts et al., 2005; Feagan et al., 2013) but cause adverse effects (Harbord et al., 2017) and fail to prevent relapses (Doherty et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Harbord et al., 2017.

claim: Current IBD therapies fail to prevent relapses.
source: Current therapies, such as anti-tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNF-α) antibodies (Rutgeerts et al., 2005) and integrin α4β7 antibodies, blocking leukocyte migration (Feagan et al., 2013), can temporarily alleviate inflammation in a subset of patients (Rutgeerts et al., 2005; Feagan et al., 2013) but cause adverse effects (Harbord et al., 2017) and fail to prevent relapses (Doherty et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Doherty et al., 2018.

claim: Heterogeneity in clinical presentations as well as diversity in diet and lifestyle among human IBD patients renders human genetic studies challenging.
source: Heterogeneity in clinical presentations as well as diversity in diet and lifestyle among human IBD patients renders human genetic studies challenging (Molodecky et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Molodecky et al., 2011.

claim: Experiments in laboratory mice allow to control several environmental factors when exploring the genetic modulators of IBD.
source: Experiments in laboratory mice allow to control several environmental factors, such as temperature and diet, when exploring the genetic modulators of IBD and also enable the collection of several relevant tissues to help elucidate tissue-specific mechanisms (Nadeau and Auwerx, 2019; Li and Auwerx, 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Nadeau and Auwerx, 2019 and Li and Auwerx, 2020.

claim: Mouse genetic reference populations (GRPs) can be used to mirror the heterogeneity of human populations in a systems genetics paradigm.
source: In addition, to mirror the heterogeneity of human populations, genetically diverse populations, such as mouse genetic reference populations (GRPs), can be used in a systems genetics paradigm (Nadeau and Auwerx, 2019; Li and Auwerx, 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Nadeau and Auwerx, 2019 and Li and Auwerx, 2020.

claim: Studies on the molecular basis of non-alcoholic fatty liver disease in the Collaborative Cross founder strains illustrated the importance of the genetic background in determining susceptibility to steatosis, hepatic inflammation, and fibrosis.
source: For example, studies on the molecular basis of non-alcoholic fatty liver disease in the Collaborative Cross founder strains illustrated the importance of the genetic background in determining susceptibility to steatosis, hepatic inflammation, and fibrosis (Benegiamo et al., 2023).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Benegiamo et al., 2023.

claim: The BXD GRP was used to identify genetic variants associated with bile acid homeostasis.
source: Moreover, the BXD GRP was used to identify genetic variants associated with metabolic phenotype variation, such as bile acid homeostasis (Li et al., 2022), lipid metabolism in plasma (Jha et al., 2018b) and liver (Jha et al., 2018a), as well as mitochondrial dysregulation (Williams et al., 2016) using GWAS or quantitative trait locus (QTL) mapping (Wu et al., 2014; Williams et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Li et al., 2022.

claim: The BXD GRP was used to identify genetic variants associated with lipid metabolism in plasma.
source: Moreover, the BXD GRP was used to identify genetic variants associated with metabolic phenotype variation, such as bile acid homeostasis (Li et al., 2022), lipid metabolism in plasma (Jha et al., 2018b) and liver (Jha et al., 2018a), as well as mitochondrial dysregulation (Williams et al., 2016) using GWAS or quantitative trait locus (QTL) mapping (Wu et al., 2014; Williams et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Jha et al., 2018b.

claim: The BXD GRP was used to identify genetic variants associated with lipid metabolism in liver.
source: Moreover, the BXD GRP was used to identify genetic variants associated with metabolic phenotype variation, such as bile acid homeostasis (Li et al., 2022), lipid metabolism in plasma (Jha et al., 2018b) and liver (Jha et al., 2018a), as well as mitochondrial dysregulation (Williams et al., 2016) using GWAS or quantitative trait locus (QTL) mapping (Wu et al., 2014; Williams et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Jha et al., 2018a.

claim: The BXD GRP was used to identify genetic variants associated with mitochondrial dysregulation.
source: Moreover, the BXD GRP was used to identify genetic variants associated with metabolic phenotype variation, such as bile acid homeostasis (Li et al., 2022), lipid metabolism in plasma (Jha et al., 2018b) and liver (Jha et al., 2018a), as well as mitochondrial dysregulation (Williams et al., 2016) using GWAS or quantitative trait locus (QTL) mapping (Wu et al., 2014; Williams et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Williams et al., 2016 and Wu et al., 2014.

claim: HFD feeding from 8 to 29 wk of age induced an IBD-like transcriptomic signature in colons of some, but not all, BXD strains.
source: HFD feeding from 8 to 29 wk of age induced an IBD-like transcriptomic signature in colons of some, but not all, BXD strains, uncovering a subset of BXD strains that could be susceptible to HFD-induced IBD-like state.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's transcriptome analysis and enrichment studies.

claim: Two IBD-related modules were identified in the colons of HFD-fed mice.
source: Gene co-expression analysis revealed two IBD-related modules in the colons of HFD-fed mice, one of which is likely under the control of a module quantitative trait locus (ModQTL).
evidence: This is a primary finding from WGCNA and ModQTL analysis.

claim: One of the IBD-related modules is likely under the control of a module quantitative trait locus (ModQTL).
source: Gene co-expression analysis revealed two IBD-related modules in the colons of HFD-fed mice, one of which is likely under the control of a module quantitative trait locus (ModQTL).
evidence: This is a finding from ModQTL mapping analysis.

claim: 115 genes were upregulated and 295 genes were downregulated by HFD in BXD colons (absolute log2(fold change) > 0.5 and BH-adjusted p-value<0.05).
source: To obtain a global, strain-independent, view of the HFD effect, we performed a differential expression analysis and identified 115 up- and 295 downregulated differentially expressed genes (DEGs, absolute log2(fold change) > 0.5 and Benjamini–Hochberg [BH]-adjusted p-value<0.05, Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a primary finding from differential expression analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Cldn4 was significantly downregulated upon HFD.
source: Of note, Cldn4, one of claudins implicated in intestinal permeability (Ahmad et al., 2017), was significantly downregulated and serum amyloid A (Saa1 and Saa3), which have been involved in the inflammatory response (Ye and Sun, 2015; Tannock et al., 2018), were upregulated upon HFD (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a specific finding from differential expression analysis shown in Figure 1B and supported by citation to Ahmad et al., 2017.

claim: Serum amyloid A (Saa1 and Saa3) were upregulated upon HFD.
source: Of note, Cldn4, one of claudins implicated in intestinal permeability (Ahmad et al., 2017), was significantly downregulated and serum amyloid A (Saa1 and Saa3), which have been involved in the inflammatory response (Ye and Sun, 2015; Tannock et al., 2018), were upregulated upon HFD (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a specific finding from differential expression analysis shown in Figure 1B and supported by citations to Ye and Sun, 2015 and Tannock et al., 2018.

claim: HFD upregulated inflammation-related pathways in BXD colons.
source: Furthermore, gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) showed an upregulation of inflammation, cell proliferation and translation, mitochondrial respiration, and stress response-related pathways upon HFD, while genes involved in the intermediate filament – that contribute to maintaining intestinal barriers (Misiorek et al., 2016; Mun et al., 2022) – were downregulated (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a finding from GSEA shown in Figure 1C.

claim: HFD upregulated translation-related pathways in BXD colons.
source: Furthermore, gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) showed an upregulation of inflammation, cell proliferation and translation, mitochondrial respiration, and stress response-related pathways upon HFD, while genes involved in the intermediate filament – that contribute to maintaining intestinal barriers (Misiorek et al., 2016; Mun et al., 2022) – were downregulated (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a finding from GSEA shown in Figure 1C.

claim: HFD upregulated mitochondrial respiration-related pathways in BXD colons.
source: Furthermore, gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) showed an upregulation of inflammation, cell proliferation and translation, mitochondrial respiration, and stress response-related pathways upon HFD, while genes involved in the intermediate filament – that contribute to maintaining intestinal barriers (Misiorek et al., 2016; Mun et al., 2022) – were downregulated (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a finding from GSEA shown in Figure 1C.

claim: HFD upregulated stress response-related pathways in BXD colons.
source: Furthermore, gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) showed an upregulation of inflammation, cell proliferation and translation, mitochondrial respiration, and stress response-related pathways upon HFD, while genes involved in the intermediate filament – that contribute to maintaining intestinal barriers (Misiorek et al., 2016; Mun et al., 2022) – were downregulated (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a finding from GSEA shown in Figure 1C.

claim: HFD downregulated intermediate filament-related genes in BXD colons.
source: Furthermore, gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) showed an upregulation of inflammation, cell proliferation and translation, mitochondrial respiration, and stress response-related pathways upon HFD, while genes involved in the intermediate filament – that contribute to maintaining intestinal barriers (Misiorek et al., 2016; Mun et al., 2022) – were downregulated (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a finding from GSEA shown in Figure 1C and supported by citations to Misiorek et al., 2016 and Mun et al., 2022.

claim: DSS-induced genes from days 4, 6 and 7 were significantly enriched in genes upregulated by HFD.
source: GSEA showed that DSS-induced genes from days 4 (early inflammatory phase), 6 and 7 (acute inflammatory phase) were significantly enriched in genes upregulated by HFD, especially the dysregulated genes in the later stage of DSS-induced UC (Figure 1D, bottom panel).
evidence: This is a finding from GSEA using DSS-induced UC signatures shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Genes involved in human IBD (UC and CDs) were enriched in genes upregulated by HFD.
source: Similarly, genes involved in human IBD (UC and CDs) were also enriched in those same genes (Figure 1D, top panel).
evidence: This is a finding from GSEA using human IBD signatures shown in Figure 1D.

claim: BXD44, 45, and 55 were the three most susceptible strains to gut inflammation upon HFD.
source: For example, BXD44, 45, and 55, highlighted in red, were the three most susceptible strains to gut inflammation upon HFD, whereas BXD1, 67, and 85, colored in green, showed no significant enrichment in gut inflammation.
evidence: This is based on strain-specific GSEA results shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: BXD1, 67, and 85 showed no significant enrichment in gut inflammation upon HFD.
source: For example, BXD44, 45, and 55, highlighted in red, were the three most susceptible strains to gut inflammation upon HFD, whereas BXD1, 67, and 85, colored in green, showed no significant enrichment in gut inflammation.
evidence: This is based on strain-specific GSEA results shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: DSS is widely used to induce UC in mouse models and disease severity increases over time.
source: DSS is widely used to induce UC in mouse models and disease severity increases over time (Czarnewski et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Czarnewski et al., 2019.

claim: Hierarchical clustering of the normalized enrichment scores (NES) in mouse IBD datasets classified the BXDs into three groups: susceptible strains (19 strains), intermediate strains (11 strains), and resistant strains (17 strains).
source: Hierarchical clustering of the normalized enrichment scores (NES) in mouse IBD datasets classified the BXDs into three groups: susceptible strains highlighted in red (19 strains), intermediate strains represented in blue (11 strains), and resistant strains colored in green (17 strains) (Figure 2A, top panel).
evidence: This is a finding from hierarchical clustering analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The C57BL/6J strain was classified as one of the susceptible strains to HFD-induced IBD-like inflammation.
source: Of note, in line with colon histological lesions comparison of DSS-induced colitis mouse models in the literature (Mähler et al., 1998), the C57BL/6J strain, one of the parental strains of the BXDs, was classified as one of the susceptible strains while the other parental strain DBA/2J belonged to the resistant group (Figure 2A, top panel), suggesting that genetic determinants inherited from the parental strains may determine the susceptibility of BXD strains to HFD-induced IBD-like inflammation in the colons.
evidence: This is a finding from the clustering analysis shown in Figure 2A and supported by citation to Mähler et al., 1998.

claim: The DBA/2J strain belonged to the resistant group to HFD-induced IBD-like inflammation.
source: Of note, in line with colon histological lesions comparison of DSS-induced colitis mouse models in the literature (Mähler et al., 1998), the C57BL/6J strain, one of the parental strains of the BXDs, was classified as one of the susceptible strains while the other parental strain DBA/2J belonged to the resistant group (Figure 2A, top panel), suggesting that genetic determinants inherited from the parental strains may determine the susceptibility of BXD strains to HFD-induced IBD-like inflammation in the colons.
evidence: This is a finding from the clustering analysis shown in Figure 2A and supported by citation to Mähler et al., 1998.

claim: The susceptible group has significantly lower levels of the anti-inflammatory cytokine IL-10 compared to the resistant strains under HFD.
source: Interestingly, the susceptible group has significantly lower levels of the anti-inflammatory cytokine–interleukin (IL)-10 (Figure 2B, two-tailed t-test p<0.01) and increased the proinflammatory cytokine–IL-15 (Figure 2C, two-tailed t-test p<0.0001) compared to the resistant strains.
evidence: This is a finding from plasma cytokine measurements shown in Figure 2B with statistical test.

claim: The susceptible group has significantly increased levels of the proinflammatory cytokine IL-15 compared to the resistant strains under HFD.
source: Interestingly, the susceptible group has significantly lower levels of the anti-inflammatory cytokine–interleukin (IL)-10 (Figure 2B, two-tailed t-test p<0.01) and increased the proinflammatory cytokine–IL-15 (Figure 2C, two-tailed t-test p<0.0001) compared to the resistant strains.
evidence: This is a finding from plasma cytokine measurements shown in Figure 2C with statistical test.

claim: IL10 has been identified as an IBD-related candidate gene using GWAS in humans.
source: IL10 itself has been identified as an IBD-related candidate gene using GWAS in humans (Franke et al., 2008) and IL-10-deficient mice are also well-known mouse model for IBD research (Keubler et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Franke et al., 2008.

claim: IL-10-deficient mice are a well-known mouse model for IBD research.
source: IL10 itself has been identified as an IBD-related candidate gene using GWAS in humans (Franke et al., 2008) and IL-10-deficient mice are also well-known mouse model for IBD research (Keubler et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Keubler et al., 2015.

claim: IL-15 is an important cytokine involved in intestinal inflammation and is elevated in the human guts with IBD.
source: IL-15 is another important cytokine involved in intestinal inflammation and is elevated in the human guts with IBD (Liu et al., 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Liu et al., 2000.

claim: IL-15 knockout mice have less severe symptoms following DSS administration.
source: IL-15 knockout mice are also reported to have less severe symptoms, such as weight loss and histological scores, following DSS administration (Yoshihara et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Yoshihara et al., 2006.

claim: The HFD co-expression network consisted of 39 modules ranging in size from 34 to 1853 genes and containing a total of 14,723 genes.
source: The HFD co-expression network consisted of 39 modules ranging in size from 34 to 1853 genes and containing a total of 14,723 genes (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a finding from WGCNA analysis.

claim: Modules HFD_M9 (484 genes), HFD_M16 (328 genes), and HFD_M28 (123 genes) were enriched with genes that are upregulated by DSS-induced colitis.
source: Enrichment analyses indicated that modules HFD_M9 (484 genes), HFD_M16 (328 genes), and HFD_M28 (123 genes) were enriched with genes that are upregulated by DSS-induced colitis, while HFD_M15 (368 genes), HFD_M24 (159 genes), and HFD_M26 (135 genes) were significantly enriched with downregulated genes (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a finding from enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Modules HFD_M15 (368 genes), HFD_M24 (159 genes), and HFD_M26 (135 genes) were significantly enriched with genes downregulated by DSS-induced colitis.
source: Enrichment analyses indicated that modules HFD_M9 (484 genes), HFD_M16 (328 genes), and HFD_M28 (123 genes) were enriched with genes that are upregulated by DSS-induced colitis, while HFD_M15 (368 genes), HFD_M24 (159 genes), and HFD_M26 (135 genes) were significantly enriched with downregulated genes (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a finding from enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: More than 20% of the genes involved in HFD_M9 and HFD_M28 were part of the dysregulated genes of the acute phase of mouse UC (days 6 and 7).
source: Of note, more than 20% of the genes involved in HFD_M9 and HFD_M28 were part of the dysregulated genes of the acute phase of mouse UC (days 6 and 7) (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a finding from enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Genes perturbed during IBD pathogenesis in humans were enriched in HFD_M9 and HFD_M28.
source: Interestingly, genes perturbed during IBD pathogenesis in humans were also enriched in HFD_M9 and HFD_M28 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a finding from enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Two modules, CD_M28 (185 genes) and CD_M32 (142 genes), in CD-fed mouse colons were associated with IBD.
source: While IBD-related genes were predominantly found in HFD modules, we also found that two modules, CD_M28 (185 genes) and CD_M32 (142 genes), in CD-fed mouse colons were associated with IBD (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a finding from enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: CD_M28 and CD_M32 significantly overlapped with the IBD-related HFD_M9 and HFD_M28 modules, respectively.
source: These two modules significantly overlapped with the IBD-related HFD_M9 and HFD_M28 modules, respectively (BH-adjusted p-value<0.05) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a finding from module overlap analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Genes in HFD_M9 were enriched in KRAS signaling and inflammation-related pathways.
source: Genes in HFD_M9 were enriched in KRAS signaling and inflammation-related pathways, while HFD_M28 was enriched in IFN-α/γ responses (BH-adjusted p-value<0.05) (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a finding from enrichment analysis using Hallmark database shown in Figure 4A.

claim: HFD_M28 was enriched in IFN-α/γ responses.
source: Genes in HFD_M9 were enriched in KRAS signaling and inflammation-related pathways, while HFD_M28 was enriched in IFN-α/γ responses (BH-adjusted p-value<0.05) (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a finding from enrichment analysis using Hallmark database shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Both HFD_M9 and HFD_M28 modules were enriched in IFN-γ response genes.
source: Both modules were enriched in IFN-γ response genes (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a finding from enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: IFN-γ is an essential cytokine for innate and adaptive intestinal immune responses.
source: IFN-γ is an essential cytokine for innate and adaptive intestinal immune responses (Brasseit et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Brasseit et al., 2018.

claim: IFN-γ plays a key role in mouse and human IBD pathogenesis.
source: It has been reported to play a key role in mouse (Ito et al., 2006) and human (Tilg et al., 2002) IBD pathogenesis, and was identified as a potential therapeutic target to alleviate inflammatory response in IBD (Li et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Ito et al., 2006 and Tilg et al., 2002.

claim: IFN-γ was identified as a potential therapeutic target to alleviate inflammatory response in IBD.
source: It has been reported to play a key role in mouse (Ito et al., 2006) and human (Tilg et al., 2002) IBD pathogenesis, and was identified as a potential therapeutic target to alleviate inflammatory response in IBD (Li et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Li et al., 2021.

claim: Genes that are dysregulated in immune cells of CDs patients (macrophages, B cell, and immune cycling cells) were enriched in HFD_M9.
source: In addition, genes that are dysregulated in immune cells of CDs patients (macrophages, B cell, and immune cycling cells) were enriched in HFD_M9 (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a finding from enrichment analysis using cell-type gene signatures shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Genes of HFD_M28 were enriched for genes that are dysregulated in immune cells and intestinal epithelial cells of diseased individuals.
source: In contrast, genes of HFD_M28 were not only enriched for genes that are dysregulated in immune cells, but also in intestinal epithelial cells of diseased individuals, such as Goblet and stem cells (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a finding from enrichment analysis using cell-type gene signatures shown in Figure 4B.

claim: ZIC2, SMAD3, REL, FOSL1, and BATF are the top enriched TFs for the genes in HFD_M9.
source: To identify transcriptional drivers of the two IBD-related modules, we performed a transcription factor (TF) enrichment analysis ('Materials and methods') and found that ZIC2, SMAD3, REL, FOSL1, and BATF are the top enriched TFs for the genes in HFD_M9 (Figure 4C), while the expression of genes in module HFD_M28 may be regulated by interferon regulatory factors (IRFs, IRF1, IRF2, IRF7, and IRF9) and the signal transducer and activator of transcription families (STAT, STAT2) (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a finding from TF enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The expression of genes in module HFD_M28 may be regulated by interferon regulatory factors (IRFs, IRF1, IRF2, IRF7, and IRF9) and STAT2.
source: To identify transcriptional drivers of the two IBD-related modules, we performed a transcription factor (TF) enrichment analysis ('Materials and methods') and found that ZIC2, SMAD3, REL, FOSL1, and BATF are the top enriched TFs for the genes in HFD_M9 (Figure 4C), while the expression of genes in module HFD_M28 may be regulated by interferon regulatory factors (IRFs, IRF1, IRF2, IRF7, and IRF9) and the signal transducer and activator of transcription families (STAT, STAT2) (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a finding from TF enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Smad3 mutant mice were more susceptible to intestinal inflammation.
source: For example, Smad3 mutant mice were more susceptible to intestinal inflammation (Yang et al., 1999).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Yang et al., 1999.

claim: The IFN-STAT axis is essential to initiate the type I IFN induction that is critical for human immune defense.
source: Moreover, the IFN-STAT axis is essential to initiate the type I IFN induction that is critical for human immune defense, such as IBD diseases (Stolzer et al., 2021) and primary immunodeficiency diseases (Mogensen, 2018), as well as for disease tolerance (Mottis et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Stolzer et al., 2021; Mogensen, 2018; and Mottis et al., 2022.

claim: A suggestive QTL for HFD_M28 was found on chromosome 16 containing 552 protein-coding genes.
source: We found a suggestive QTL for HFD_M28 (p-value<0.1) on chromosome 16 containing 552 protein-coding genes (Figure 5A, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a finding from ModQTL mapping analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: No significant or suggestive QTLs were detected for modules that are significantly enriched in IBD-downregulated genes (HFD_M15, HFD_M24, and HFD_M26).
source: The ModQTL analysis was also performed on the modules that are significantly enriched in IBD-downregulated genes (HFD_M15, HFD_M24, and HFD_M26), but no significant or suggestive QTLs were detected.
evidence: This is a finding from ModQTL mapping analysis.

claim: 27 genes satisfying at least two of the filtering criteria were considered as candidate genes driving the expression of module HFD_M28.
source: The 27 genes satisfying at least two of the above criteria were considered as candidate genes driving the expression of module HFD_M28 (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a finding from the candidate gene prioritization scheme shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Genetic variants of EPHA6 were associated with UC in humans (p-value=2.3E-06).
source: Interestingly, the genetic variants of two genes under the QTL peak, that is, ephrin type A receptor 6 (EPHA6, p-value=2.3E-06) (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, Supplementary file 3) and Mucin 4 (MUC4, p-value=1.2E-06) (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B, Supplementary file 4) were also associated with UC in humans.
evidence: This is a finding from GWAS in UKBB shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Genetic variants of MUC4 were associated with UC in humans (p-value=1.2E-06).
source: Interestingly, the genetic variants of two genes under the QTL peak, that is, ephrin type A receptor 6 (EPHA6, p-value=2.3E-06) (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, Supplementary file 3) and Mucin 4 (MUC4, p-value=1.2E-06) (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B, Supplementary file 4) were also associated with UC in humans.
evidence: This is a finding from GWAS in UKBB shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: EPHA6 belongs to Eph/Ephrin Signaling, and this pathway has been associated with gut inflammation.
source: EPHA6 belongs to Eph/Ephrin Signaling, and this pathway has been associated with gut inflammation (Coulthard et al., 2012) and proposed as a potential target to alleviate the inflammatory response in IBD (Grandi et al., 2019), but the association between EPHA6 and IBD is not explored yet.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Coulthard et al., 2012.

claim: Eph/Ephrin Signaling has been proposed as a potential target to alleviate the inflammatory response in IBD.
source: EPHA6 belongs to Eph/Ephrin Signaling, and this pathway has been associated with gut inflammation (Coulthard et al., 2012) and proposed as a potential target to alleviate the inflammatory response in IBD (Grandi et al., 2019), but the association between EPHA6 and IBD is not explored yet.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Grandi et al., 2019.

claim: Expression of Epha6 in mouse gastrointestinal tract correlates with genes involved in inflammation-related pathways, such as IL-6 production and regulation of inflammatory response.
source: The Gene-Module Association Determination (G-MAD) (Li et al., 2019; https://systems-genetics.org/gmad) also revealed that expression of Epha6 in mouse gastrointestinal tract correlates with genes involved in inflammation-related pathways, such as IL-6 production and regulation of inflammatory response (Figure 5D, Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is a finding from G-MAD analysis shown in Figure 5D and supported by citation to Li et al., 2019.

claim: MUC4 is a transmembrane mucin.
source: MUC4 is a transmembrane mucin (Gao et al., 2021) and highly expressed in gastrointestinal tract according to the human protein atlas (Uhlén et al., 2015; https://www.proteinatlas.org/humanproteome/tissue/intestine; Figure 5C).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Gao et al., 2021.

claim: MUC4 is highly expressed in gastrointestinal tract according to the human protein atlas.
source: MUC4 is a transmembrane mucin (Gao et al., 2021) and highly expressed in gastrointestinal tract according to the human protein atlas (Uhlén et al., 2015; https://www.proteinatlas.org/humanproteome/tissue/intestine; Figure 5C).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Uhlén et al., 2015 and data from the human protein atlas shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The expression of MUC4 in the human gastrointestinal tract correlates with genes that are enriched for CRC and O-linked glycosylation.
source: The expression of MUC4 in the human gastrointestinal tract correlates with genes that are enriched for CRC and O-linked glycosylation based on G-MAD (Li et al., 2019; Figure 5E, Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is a finding from G-MAD analysis shown in Figure 5E and supported by citation to Li et al., 2019.

claim: O-linked glycans are expressed by the intestinal epithelium to maintain barrier function.
source: O-linked glycans are expressed by the intestinal epithelium to maintain barrier function, especially mucin type O-glycans, and gut disorders can be affected by dysfunction of O-linked glycosylation (Brazil and Parkos, 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Brazil and Parkos, 2022.

claim: Gut disorders can be affected by dysfunction of O-linked glycosylation.
source: O-linked glycans are expressed by the intestinal epithelium to maintain barrier function, especially mucin type O-glycans, and gut disorders can be affected by dysfunction of O-linked glycosylation (Brazil and Parkos, 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Brazil and Parkos, 2022.

claim: MUC4 is upregulated in enterocytes and Goblet cells in colons of CDs patients.
source: Moreover, MUC4 is upregulated in enterocytes and Goblet cells in colons of CDs patients (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5F based on cell-type specific expression data.

claim: MUC4 has a role in maintaining the intestinal epithelium and controlling the gut inflammatory response.
source: MUC4 hence is a strong candidate because of its role in maintaining the intestinal epithelium and controlling the gut inflammatory response (McGuckin et al., 2011) and EPHA6 might be a novel candidate gene to impact gut inflammation.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to McGuckin et al., 2011.

claim: MUC4 has cis-eQTLs in the sigmoid and transverse colon.
source: To test this possibility, we examined the GTEx resource (Lonsdale et al., 2013) and found that MUC4, but not EPHA6, has cis-eQTLs in the sigmoid and transverse colon.
evidence: This is a finding from examining GTEx data and supported by citation to Lonsdale et al., 2013.

claim: EPHA6 does not have cis-eQTLs in the sigmoid and transverse colon.
source: To test this possibility, we examined the GTEx resource (Lonsdale et al., 2013) and found that MUC4, but not EPHA6, has cis-eQTLs in the sigmoid and transverse colon.
evidence: This is a finding from examining GTEx data and supported by citation to Lonsdale et al., 2013.

claim: Increased expression of MUC4 in the sigmoid colon may increase the risk of IBD (nominal p-value=0.033).
source: Using publicly available GWAS summary statistics for IBD, CDs, and UC (Liu et al., 2015; Elsworth et al., 2020) as outcomes, we found suggestive evidence that increased expression of MUC4 in the sigmoid, but not transverse, colon may increase the risk of IBD (nominal p-value=0.033, Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This is a finding from Mendelian randomization analysis using GWAS summary statistics from Liu et al., 2015 and Elsworth et al., 2020.

claim: Muc4 knockout mice have been shown to be more resistant to DSS-induced UC through upregulating the expression of Muc2 and Muc3.
source: Furthermore, Muc4 knockout mice have been shown to be more resistant to DSS-induced UC through upregulating the expression of Muc2 (mucin secretion) and Muc3 (transmembrane mucin) (Das et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Das et al., 2016.

claim: A GWAS indicated that mutations in EPHA6 increase risk for CRC.
source: A GWAS also indicated that mutations in EPHA6 increase risk for CRC (Guda et al., 2015), but its potential association with IBD is a new finding.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Guda et al., 2015.

claim: The colon transcriptomic response to HFD in the BXD mouse population recapitulated several of the general features observed in DSS-induced UC mouse models and human IBD patients.
source: The colon transcriptomic response to HFD in this mouse population recapitulated several of the general features observed in DSS-induced UC mouse models and human IBD patients.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the study's findings based on enrichment analyses.

claim: The upregulation of inflammation-related genes and the UPR as well as the downregulation of intercellular adhesion-related genesets are common signatures induced by HFD.
source: In particular, we identified the upregulation of inflammation-related genes and the UPR as well as the downregulation of intercellular adhesion-related genesets as common signatures induced by HFD (Kreuter, 2019).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the study and supported by citation to Kreuter, 2019.

claim: Susceptibility groups differed in anti- and pro-inflammatory plasma cytokine levels (IL-10 and IL-15, respectively).
source: The fact that these susceptibility groups also differed in anti- and pro-inflammatory plasma cytokine levels (IL-10 and IL-15, respectively) suggests a relation between these tissue-specific transcriptional signatures and systemic low-grade inflammation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cytokine measurements shown in Figures 2B and 2C.

claim: Gene interactions determine cellular processes and the molecular functions of correlated genes are often similar.
source: Since gene interactions determine cellular processes and the molecular functions of correlated genes are often similar (Nayak et al., 2009), we attempted to elucidate the mechanism underlying the diversity of IBD-like signatures and chronic inflammation in BXD colons using gene co-expression analyses.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Nayak et al., 2009.

claim: Most differentially expressed genes are likely to be driven by and not be a cause of disease.
source: As most differentially expressed genes are likely to be driven by and not be a cause of disease (Porcu et al., 2021), we attempted to understand whether the signatures in the colon are causes or consequences of chronic inflammation.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Porcu et al., 2021.

claim: Both IBD-associated modules largely consisted of immune response-related genes.
source: Enrichment analyses showed that both IBD-associated modules largely consisted of immune response-related genes.
evidence: This is a summary of enrichment analysis findings shown in Figure 4A and 4B.

claim: Genes involved in HFD_M9 and HFD_M28 are both differentially expressed in immune cells in inflamed tissues of CDs patients.
source: Specifically, genes involved in HFD_M9 and HFD_M28 are both differentially expressed in immune cells in inflamed tissues of CDs patients (Kong et al., 2023).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Kong et al., 2023.

claim: Genetic determinants inherited from the parental strains may determine the susceptibility of BXD strains to HFD-induced IBD-like inflammation in the colons.
source: Of note, in line with colon histological lesions comparison of DSS-induced colitis mouse models in the literature (Mähler et al., 1998), the C57BL/6J strain, one of the parental strains of the BXDs, was classified as one of the susceptible strains while the other parental strain DBA/2J belonged to the resistant group (Figure 2A, top panel), suggesting that genetic determinants inherited from the parental strains may determine the susceptibility of BXD strains to HFD-induced IBD-like inflammation in the colons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the classification of parental strains and supported by citation to Mähler et al., 1998.

claim: Chronic inflammation induced upon HFD feeding may be a prelude to human UC.
source: In support of the generalizability of our data, the identified candidate genes in our mouse models were also associated to human UC, demonstrating that chronic inflammation induced upon HFD feeding may indeed be a prelude to human UC.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the validation of candidate genes in human GWAS.
